video_title: Lawfare Daily: Why Autocrats Hate Cities with Ambassador Nina Hachigian
transcript: It's the LawFare podcast. I'm Tyler McBryan, managing editor of Lawfair with Ambassador Nina Hachigian, president and CEO of the Alliance for Local Leaders International and the first US Special Representative for City and State Diplomacy from 2022 to 2025. They are little democracies with three branches of government with rights guaranteed with transparency and accountability and responsiveness and tangible progress, tangible delivery of what people need and want and that keeps our norms somewhat preserved. Today we're talking about the ambassador's recent piece in Foreign Affairs entitled The Autocrat's Worst Enemy. We discussed how cities are both laboratories of democracy and backs stops against democratic backsliding as well as what US mayors can learn about resisting autocracy from their counterparts abroad. So ambassador, I wanted to start, if I may, with a bit about your background and the origins of your interest in this relationship between cities, democracy, international affairs, diplomacy. Um, in other words, why did you write this? Yeah, thank you for the questions. I had a kind of relatively traditional career in foreign policy was, you know, worked at think tanks and then was lucky to be an ambassador under President Obama and then I came back to the US and got a an offer I couldn't refuse from Mayor Eric Garcetti of Los Angeles to be his first deputy mayor of international affairs. And in that job, I learned about just the incredible power of cities, both in improving the lives of the residents of the city, but also in how they network internationally and learn a tremendous amount from each other. So, I'll give you two examples of that. So, one, um, the mayor took a trip to Mexico City. We have a sister city relationship with Mexico City. This is before I came on board. And he met with Claudia Shangbomb. now the president of Mexico and noticed there that they had this earthquake early warning system that that she told them about. So he came back to Los Angeles and said we need to have an earthquake early warning system. And so the city worked on that and and set it up. So now that you know you have residents in Los Angeles who have a few seconds to, you know, jump under a table before the earthquake hits. And then this the state since adopted it. So now we have 40 million residents of California who all can have this app on their phone that gives them a little time. So that's one example. Another is that he was chair of a group called C40 and that is the 100 or so biggest cities of the world all of whom have pledged to to attack climate change because of the terrible effects it was having in all their cities. Uh floods you know heat I don't have to go through it and expensive energy. And so that collective has done a tremendous amount toward taking carbon out of the atmosphere. And when you think about it, cities, you know, they have public transit that's if you electrify your public transit, you know, that's a big step. You can divert your organic waste and that doesn't then you don't create methane, which is worse than carbon, etc., etc. So those are two kinds of examples of how cities work internationally. So that was that. And then I got a chance to do that work in the Biden administration, but not just for Los Angeles, but for all cities in the United States. And then we did a lot of connectivity, not actually just cities, cities and states and counties and the the whole lot. And in that job, we did a lot of connecting across borders for learning, for shared problem solving, etc. And you know, we reached I think something like 5,000 local leaders and answered lots of questions and helped them with their own international plans. I was expecting the biggest surprise of that job. I was expecting, you know, I'm coming from Los Angeles, big global city, but there is interest across the United States in some of the smallest towns and cities in international work. But anyway, in that role, we did some a bunch of work on democracy. And so I was aware I became aware of how cities can preserve and exercise and innovate the systems of democracy. The kinds of things that we take for granted like guaranteeing people's freedoms, you know, issuing permits protest and monitoring elections and working with civil society and being transparent and trying to be responsive to people's needs quickly and tangibly. All of that's democracy and it happens in these many democracies all around the world. >> Thank you for that. That's a really helpful setup and we will definitely dig into a lot of that municipal multilateralism as uh you refer to it in your piece. And before we dig into the meat of your argument in your foreign affairs piece, I'm hoping you could um shed a little light on what happens in these offices of international affairs. Um it's something that I've been curious about. Well, sadly in the United States, the capacity for this international engagement is actually quite uh limited. So, you you're pointed out that Los Angeles and and New York have the biggest offices. Uh New York has a lovely new commissioner. I really like her. She's really smart. A commissioner of international affairs and she's got a great team. And similarly with LA and then it's like you know Seattle has one person, Atlanta may have a few, San Antonio has one person like these big cities Chicago has one person and then most places have nobody and they're just you know the chief of staff is doing it or you know someone else maybe occasionally you've got someone in the economic development department who is doing these issues. So, a day in the life really changes depending on what kind of city you're talking about. And let me just draw a contrast here because Tokyo has like 50 people doing international affairs and Shanghai has 100 and even Bonosades has like 20. So we really I mean in general we underresource cities in the United States and when it comes to international engagement you know there's there's just no there there are very few cities that can afford to reap the benefits of someone who's doing international work. It could be that we are trying to attract businesses uh foreign businesses to set up.
